laws.fullDescription: The Bank of Japan ended its negative interest rate policy in March 2024 and raised rates for the first time in 17 years, responding to inflation finally reaching target levels. The yen had depreciated dramatically, hitting 160 per dollar, prompting government intervention. The policy shift marked a historic end to Japan's decades-long deflation fight.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; financial regulatory adjustments
exceptions: Gradual rate adjustment to protect fragile recovery
Government bond market stability requirements

quiz.q: What historic monetary policy did the Bank of Japan end in March 2024?
quiz.explanation: The Bank of Japan ended its negative interest rate policy in March 2024 and raised rates for the first time in 17 years, marking a historic shift in monetary policy.

laws.title: Aging Society Workforce Integration Reforms
laws.subtitle: Japan Extends Working Age and Attracts Foreign Workers
laws.fullDescription: Japan continued expanding workforce participation of elderly workers and foreign nationals in response to its severe labor shortage driven by demographic decline. The government raised the standard employment age to 70 and streamlined skilled worker visa categories. Japan remained culturally cautious about immigration even while expanding practical pathways.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; employment age discrimination prohibited
exceptions: Mandatory retirement ages phased out
Skilled specific industries track

quiz.q: To what age did Japan raise the standard employment age?
quiz.explanation: Japan raised the standard employment age to 70 in response to its severe labor shortage driven by demographic decline and low immigration historically.

laws.title: LDP Black Money Scandal and Political Reform
laws.subtitle: Japan's Ruling Party Hit By Slush Fund Revelations
laws.fullDescription: Japan's Liberal Democratic Party faced its worst political crisis in decades when revelations emerged that factions had maintained slush funds of unreported political donations exceeding 500 million yen. Multiple LDP executives were arrested or resigned. The scandal contributed to PM Kishida's resignation and reduced the LDP's parliamentary majority.
laws.penalty: Criminal charges for political fund law violations; fines
exceptions: Voluntary disclosure reduced charges
Political fund reform legislation

quiz.q: What political scandal contributed to Japan PM Kishida's resignation?
options: LDP slush fund revelations with unreported donations
quiz.explanation: LDP factions' slush fund scandal, involving unreported political donations exceeding 500 million yen, contributed to PM Kishida's resignation and severely damaged the ruling party.

laws.title: Offshore Wind Expansion and Green Transformation Act
laws.subtitle: Japan Accelerates Renewable Energy After Nuclear Pause
laws.fullDescription: Japan expanded offshore wind development under the Act on Promoting Use of Sea Areas for Marine Renewable Energy Power Generation, designating major zones for development. Japan aimed to install 10 GW of offshore wind by 2030 and 30-45 GW by 2040. The push came alongside restarting some nuclear plants.
laws.penalty: Development zone application compliance; environmental assessment requirements
exceptions: Fishing community consultation requirements
Defense zone exclusions

quiz.q: How much offshore wind capacity does Japan aim to install by 2030?
quiz.explanation: Japan aims to install 10 GW of offshore wind by 2030 and 30-45 GW by 2040 under its Marine Renewable Energy Act.

laws.title: Japan's Semiconductor Renaissance and Chip Industry Revival
laws.subtitle: Japan attracts TSMC and rebuilds strategic semiconductor manufacturing
laws.fullDescription: Japan has launched a major effort to rebuild its semiconductor industry after decades of decline. TSMC built its first overseas factory in Kumamoto, Japan, with massive Japanese government subsidies. Rapidus, a Japanese consortium, aims to produce cutting-edge 2nm chips by 2027. Japan's strategy combines attracting foreign chipmakers with developing domestic capabilities. The effort is driven by supply chain security concerns and geopolitical tensions over Taiwan.
laws.penalty: Companies receiving government semiconductor subsidies must maintain domestic production for minimum 10 years
exceptions: R&D facilities exempt from production continuity requirements
University research partnerships have different IP and commercialization rules

laws.title: LDP Political Funds Scandal and Coalition Government
laws.subtitle: Japan's LDP loses supermajority as slush fund scandal damages ruling party
laws.fullDescription: Japan's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), which has governed Japan for most of the postwar period, suffered a major political scandal involving undisclosed political fundraising slush funds. The 2024 elections cost the LDP its parliamentary majority, forcing a minority government or coalition. Kishida resigned; Ishiba Shigeru became PM. Japan's politics are undergoing unusual change for a country known for LDP dominance. Policy continuity on defense and economics remains despite political upheaval. The scandal spurred political finance reform demands.
laws.penalty: Unreported political fundraising funds trigger criminal prosecution under Political Funds Control Act
exceptions: Small political party fundraising under reporting thresholds has lighter requirements
Publicly funded political party subsidies exempt from private fundraising restrictions

laws.title: Robot Revolution and Labor Shortage Solution
laws.subtitle: Japan deploys industrial and service robots to address aging workforce
laws.fullDescription: Japan has the world's oldest population and a severe labor shortage. The country deploys more industrial robots per worker than any other nation and is pioneering service robots — care robots for elderly, restaurant service robots, and agricultural robots. Companies like Fanuc, Yaskawa, and Kawasaki Heavy Industries produce world-leading industrial robots. Japan's robot strategy serves two purposes: maintaining productivity with fewer workers and exporting robot technology globally as the world ages.
laws.penalty: Workplace safety regulations govern robot-human interaction in industrial settings
exceptions: Research and development robot deployments have lighter safety certification requirements
Agricultural robot use in rural areas has simplified licensing compared to industrial settings

quiz.q: Why does Japan prioritize robot deployment more than other countries?
options: Lower robot production costs as a manufacturing hub
World's oldest population combined with severe labor shortage
Cultural tradition of robot development since WWII
Government subsidies making robots cheaper than workers
quiz.explanation: Japan has both the world's oldest population and one of the most severe labor shortages — making robot automation not just efficient but existentially necessary for maintaining economic productivity.

laws.title: Inbound Tourism Boom and Overtourism Management
laws.subtitle: Japan achieves record 35 million tourists while managing overtourism
laws.fullDescription: Japan achieved record international tourism of 35+ million visitors in 2023-24 as the cheap yen attracted global visitors. Famous sites (Kyoto, Fuji, Osaka's Dotonbori) face severe overtourism. Mount Fuji implemented barriers blocking photography spots and visitor caps. Kyoto charges additional taxes on tourists. Japan's tourism boom creates both economic opportunity and quality-of-life challenges for residents. The government balances promoting high-spending tourists versus managing crowd impacts. Japan's 2030 target is 60 million visitors.
laws.penalty: Overcrowded tourist areas implement entry fees and crowd management systems
exceptions: Religious observances and festival participants have different access than standard tourists
Residents and local workers have bypass access to tourist-congested areas

quiz.q: What crowd control measure did Mount Fuji implement for overtourism?
options: Barriers blocking famous photography spots and visitor caps
Requiring professional guides for all climbers
quiz.explanation: Mount Fuji installed barriers blocking the famous 'Lawson convenience store' photography spot and implemented daily visitor caps on climbing routes — practical responses to overwhelming tourist numbers disrupting local life.

laws.title: Robot Labor and Automation Response to Aging Workforce
laws.subtitle: Japan's technological solutions to demographic decline
laws.fullDescription: Japan's rapidly aging and shrinking population has accelerated automation adoption more than almost any other country. With a fertility rate of approximately 1.2 and a population already declining, Japan faces labor shortages across nearly all sectors. The country has deployed robots in manufacturing, logistics, elder care, agriculture, and service industries at a rate that far exceeds global averages. The government actively supports robotics R&D and has eased regulations on autonomous systems. However, Japanese social attitudes have been more accepting of human-robot interaction than Western counterparts — robots that assist elderly people or serve in restaurants are not seen as dystopian. Companies like SoftBank (Pepper robot), Toyota, Honda, and dozens of startups lead global robotics innovation. Despite automation, labor shortages remain severe, prompting controversial immigration policy changes. Japan's experience is being studied as a model (or warning) for other aging societies.
laws.penalty: Labor safety regulations apply to workplaces with robotics; product liability law covers robot-caused injuries
exceptions: Medical robots face additional FDA-equivalent approval processes before clinical use

quiz.q: What is Japan's approximate current fertility rate driving its labor shortage and automation push?
quiz.explanation: Japan's fertility rate of approximately 1.2 — well below the 2.1 replacement level — has created severe labor shortages that have accelerated automation adoption across all economic sectors.

laws.title: Defense Normalization and Constitutional Reinterpretation
laws.subtitle: Japan abandoning post-WWII military restraints amid China threat
laws.fullDescription: Japan has undergone the most significant transformation of its defense posture since World War II. The government has reinterpreted Article 9 of the pacifist constitution to allow collective self-defense (defending allies under attack), doubled the defense budget to 2% of GDP over five years, and developed counterattack capabilities (previously avoided as offensive weapons). Japan has acquired long-range missiles capable of striking adversary territory — a capability that would have been constitutionally impossible under previous interpretations. Japan has deepened defense cooperation with the US, Australia, South Korea (partially overcoming historical tensions), and the Philippines. The North Korean missile program and China's military modernization have driven public support for these changes. Japan is also a founding member of the Quad security dialogue and participates in exercises with Western navies.
laws.penalty: Japan's Self-Defense Forces operate under strictly defined laws; constitutional constraints remain on formal war-making
exceptions: The reinterpreted collective self-defense allows some military cooperation previously prohibited

quiz.q: What percentage of GDP is Japan targeting for defense spending — double the previous level?
quiz.explanation: Japan is doubling its defense budget from 1% to 2% of GDP over five years — a dramatic change from the self-imposed restraint that had kept Japan's military spending at 1% of GDP since World War II.

laws.title: Yen Carry Trade Unwind Crisis
laws.subtitle: Currency volatility shakes global markets from Tokyo
laws.fullDescription: Japan's decades-low interest rates made the yen a global carry trade currency—investors borrowed cheap yen to invest in higher-yielding assets worldwide. When the Bank of Japan began hiking rates in 2024, yen appreciation triggered a massive carry trade unwind in August 2024, causing a global stock market flash crash. The Nikkei fell 12% in a single day, its worst since 1987. Japan's monetary policy became a systemic global risk, complicating the Bank of Japan's normalization path.
laws.penalty: No specific penalty but Bank of Japan must communicate rate changes carefully to prevent disorderly market unwinds
exceptions: BOJ retains full monetary policy independence
Emergency market stabilization tools available if crisis escalates

quiz.q: How much did Japan's Nikkei stock index fall in the August 2024 carry trade unwind?
quiz.explanation: The Nikkei fell 12% in a single day during the August 2024 carry trade unwind triggered by Bank of Japan rate hikes, making it the worst single-day decline since 1987.

laws.title: Wage Growth and Inflation Cycle Breaking
laws.subtitle: Japan ends 30 years of deflation with historic pay rises
laws.fullDescription: Japan's spring 2024 wage negotiations (shunto) produced the highest wage increases in 33 years, with major companies offering average raises of over 5%. The Bank of Japan raised interest rates for the first time since 2007, marking a historic shift from its ultra-loose monetary policy. These changes represented potential breaking of Japan's deflationary spiral that had persisted since the 1990s asset bubble collapse. Whether the changes would become self-sustaining or fade was the central economic question for Japan in 2025.
laws.penalty: Bank of Japan's rate changes affect all variable-rate loans; mortgage holders face increased payments as rates normalize
exceptions: Long-term fixed rate mortgages protected from rate increases
Small businesses have separate low-rate financing facilities

quiz.q: Japan's 2024 spring wage negotiations produced the highest wage increases in how many years?
quiz.explanation: Japan's 2024 shunto (spring wage negotiations) produced the highest average wage increases in 33 years, representing a potential historic break from the deflationary cycle that had gripped Japan since the 1990s bubble collapse.

laws.title: Robot Industry and Workforce Automation
laws.subtitle: Japan leads service robot deployment to offset demographic decline
laws.fullDescription: Japan is the world's leading deployer of service robots, driven by necessity as its aging and shrinking workforce cannot fill all needed positions. Robots assist in elder care, restaurant service, manufacturing, security and logistics. Japan accounts for about half of global industrial robot production. Sony, Honda (ASIMO), and numerous specialized companies develop humanoid and specialized robots. The government has explicitly encouraged robot deployment as a workforce substitute given resistance to immigration as an alternative solution.
laws.penalty: Robots operating in public spaces must meet safety certification requirements; liability for robot actions being clarified through court decisions
exceptions: Industrial robots in closed manufacturing environments have different safety standards
Research and development robots exempt from consumer-facing requirements

quiz.q: Approximately what share of global industrial robot production does Japan account for?
quiz.explanation: Japan accounts for approximately half of global industrial robot production and is the world's leading deployer of service robots—driven by an aging, shrinking workforce and cultural resistance to immigration as an alternative solution.

laws.title: Toyota Hybrid Defense and EV Hesitation
laws.subtitle: Japan's largest company bets on hybrids while rivals go pure EV
laws.fullDescription: Toyota has been more cautious about the all-electric vehicle transition than Western rivals, doubling down on hybrid technology (which it pioneered with Prius) while critics accused it of lobbying against ambitious EV mandates. Toyota argues that hybrids provide immediate emissions reductions across different markets while global electricity grids decarbonize. However Toyota has also invested in solid-state battery technology promising superior range. The company's EV hesitation has cost it market share in China's booming EV market where BYD and Chinese brands now dominate.
laws.penalty: Toyota must comply with emission standards in each market; Japan's fuel economy regulations less strict than EU or California
exceptions: Commercial vehicles have different emission standards than passenger cars
Plug-in hybrids counted differently toward zero emission targets in different jurisdictions

quiz.q: Which Toyota model pioneered mass-market hybrid vehicles that Toyota now defends against pure EV mandates?
quiz.explanation: The Toyota Prius pioneered mass-market hybrid vehicles, and Toyota's defense of hybrid technology against pure EV mandates is rooted in the company's leadership in this technology—though critics argue hybrids are a delay tactic rather than a genuine climate solution.

laws.title: Green Transformation (GX) Plan
laws.subtitle: $1 Trillion Climate Investment
laws.fullDescription: Japan's Green Transformation (GX) plan, announced in 2023, commits ¥150 trillion ($1 trillion) over 10 years to decarbonize the economy. Japan set a 46% emissions reduction by 2030 and carbon neutrality by 2050. After the 2011 Fukushima disaster shut down nuclear plants, Japan increased fossil fuel use; the GX plan involves restarting and building new nuclear plants alongside massive renewable expansion. Japan also passed the GX Promotion Act creating a carbon emission trading scheme and GX economy transition bonds. Japan leads in hydrogen technology development.
laws.penalty: ETS compliance costs; fines for major industrial emitters failing sector reduction targets
exceptions: Nuclear facilities under special regulatory framework
Defense industries
Certain critical manufacturing under strategic exemptions

laws.title: Japanese Universal Healthcare and Longevity
laws.subtitle: World's Longest-Lived Nation
laws.fullDescription: Japan's universal healthcare system (achieved 1961) covers all residents through either employer-based health insurance or National Health Insurance for the self-employed and retirees. Japan's healthcare success is remarkable: world-leading life expectancy (84+ years), among the world's lowest infant mortality, and some of the best cancer outcomes. Japan has the world's highest proportion of elderly (28%+ over 65), creating enormous pressure on its healthcare system. Japan has extraordinarily high per-capita MRI and CT scanner rates, and pioneered robotic surgery. End-of-life care and dementia care are major challenges.
laws.penalty: All residents must enroll in health insurance; employers liable; self-employed in National Health Insurance; fines for non-enrollment
exceptions: Short-term visitors under tourist health protocols
Foreign workers must enroll after 2 months

laws.title: Japan Work Style Reform and Karoshi Prevention
laws.subtitle: Fighting Death by Overwork
laws.fullDescription: Japan enacted the Work Style Reform Act (2019) — a historic shift addressing karoshi (death from overwork). The law introduced mandatory paid vacation use (at least 5 days/year must be taken), overtime caps (720 hours/year for general workers, 960 for special cases), and required equal pay for equal work between regular and non-regular employees. Japan's labor shortage has fundamentally changed the market — with labor force shrinking, employers must compete for workers. Japan has 2.1 million 'freelance' gig workers, and legislation has been proposed to extend worker protections to this group.
laws.penalty: Overtime cap violations: up to 6 months imprisonment and ¥300,000 fine; paid leave violations: fines
exceptions: Doctors have extended overtime caps until 2035
High-income professionals ('specialist work-style'): exempt from caps

laws.title: University Entrance Examination Reform
laws.subtitle: Japan's shift from rote learning to competency testing
laws.fullDescription: Japan's 2021 introduction of the Common Test for University Admissions (大学入学共通テスト) replaced the 30-year-old Center Test, emphasizing critical thinking over memorization. The Basic Act on Education (revised 2006) underpins Japan's education philosophy, requiring nine years of compulsory schooling. Japan also mandates moral education (道徳) as a formal graded subject since 2018, a controversial policy critics say promotes nationalism.
laws.penalty: Schools not providing compulsory education face administrative action; parents of truant children counseled then potentially fined
exceptions: International schools may follow foreign curricula
Special needs students receive individualized plans

quiz.q: What replaced Japan's Center Test for university admissions in 2021?
quiz.explanation: The 大学入学共通テスト (Daigaku Nyūgaku Kyōtsū Tesuto) replaced the Center Test starting January 2021, with new question formats emphasizing reading comprehension and reasoning over rote recall.

laws.title: Specified Skilled Worker Visa
laws.subtitle: Japan's reluctant opening to immigration
laws.fullDescription: Japan, facing severe demographic decline, created the Specified Skilled Worker (SSW) visa in 2019 in two tiers: SSW-1 for sectors with labor shortages (14 sectors including restaurants, nursing care, construction) and SSW-2 for higher skills with pathway to permanent residency. Japan has historically maintained very limited immigration and a racial-ethnic concept of nationality, with naturalization rare and difficult. Japan's 2024 immigration reforms expanded the SSW-2 pathway, acknowledging demographic reality. Japan had ~3 million foreign residents (2.3% of population) — low by developed country standards.
laws.penalty: Visa overstaying is a criminal offense leading to detention and 5-year re-entry ban; employers violating foreign worker conditions face license revocation; human trafficking carries up to 7 years imprisonment
exceptions: Nikkei (ethnic Japanese descendants) from Brazil, Peru have special long-term residency visa
Highly skilled professionals (HSP) get accelerated permanent residency in 1-3 years
Refugees granted status receive permanent residency
laws.sourceLabel: Japan Immigration Services Agency – Specified Skilled Worker Visa

quiz.q: Japan's 2019 Specified Skilled Worker visa was created to address what demographic problem?
options: Severe labor shortages due to aging population and low birth rate
Brain drain of Japanese workers abroad
quiz.explanation: Japan created the SSW visa as a reluctant response to severe labor shortages caused by its aging population and world's lowest birth rate. Despite cultural resistance to immigration, economic necessity drove the policy change.

laws.title: Cannabis Control Act
laws.subtitle: Japan's strict cannabis laws and recent reform debate
laws.fullDescription: Japan's Cannabis Control Act criminalizes cannabis possession, cultivation, and trafficking strictly. Japan has historically had very low drug use and harsh enforcement. Cannabis possession carries up to 5 years; trafficking up to 7 years. Japan amended the Cannabis Control Act in 2023 to allow medical cannabis use (previously even medical was banned), amid international pressure and pharmaceutical research needs. Japan arrests hundreds of celebrities and athletes for cannabis annually — often ruining careers over small amounts. Methamphetamine (shabu) is a more significant drug problem historically.
laws.penalty: Cannabis possession: up to 5 years; cannabis trafficking: up to 7 years; stimulant (methamphetamine) possession: up to 10 years; stimulant trafficking: up to 20 years; opium offenses: up to 10 years
exceptions: Medical cannabis use/research allowed since 2023 amendment
Narcotics (opioids) available by medical prescription for pain management
Hemp fiber and seed oil products regulated separately
laws.sourceLabel: Japan Cannabis Control Act and 2023 Amendment

quiz.q: Japan's 2023 amendment to the Cannabis Control Act introduced what change?
options: Allowing medical use/research of cannabis (previously fully banned)
quiz.explanation: Japan's 2023 Cannabis Control Act amendment allowed medical use of cannabis for the first time, including pharmaceutical cannabis products. Previously, even medical or research use was prohibited — an extreme restriction even by international standards.

laws.title: No National Marriage Equality — Local Partnerships Growing
laws.subtitle: Japan lacks federal same-sex marriage but court rulings and municipal partnerships are expanding
laws.fullDescription: Japan has no national recognition of same-sex relationships, but dozens of municipalities and prefectures now issue partnership certificates with some local benefits. In 2021, several district courts ruled that denying same-sex marriage is unconstitutional. The ruling coalition (LDP) has resisted national legislation. A 2023 Supreme Court ruling found the lack of any legal framework for same-sex couples unconstitutional. Japan decriminalized homosexuality in 1880 under the Meiji-era penal code. Anti-discrimination laws do not specifically cover sexual orientation at the national level.
laws.penalty: No national anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ+ individuals; local ordinances vary by municipality
exceptions: Local partnership certificates provide limited benefits without national legal force

quiz.q: What have Japanese courts increasingly ruled regarding the ban on same-sex marriage?
quiz.explanation: Since 2021, multiple Japanese district courts have ruled that denying same-sex marriage is unconstitutional, culminating in a 2023 Supreme Court finding, though national legislation has not followed.

laws.title: Press Club System Restricts Independent Journalism
laws.subtitle: Japan has constitutional press freedom but the 'kisha club' system limits access and diversity
laws.fullDescription: Japan's constitution (Article 21) guarantees freedom of expression and no censorship. Japan has a mature press with major outlets like Asahi Shimbun, Yomiuri Shimbun, NHK, and regional papers. However, Japan's 'kisha club' (press club) system restricts press access — only established outlets accredited to specific clubs can attend government briefings, creating an oligopoly of access. Freelancers and foreign correspondents face significant disadvantages. Japan has criminal defamation laws including 'insult' offenses (with prison terms added in 2022). Japan ranks in the middle globally for press freedom.
laws.penalty: Criminal defamation and 'insult' laws (insult offense: up to 1 year imprisonment after 2022 amendment); kisha club access restrictions
exceptions: Online media has grown outside the kisha club system

quiz.q: What is Japan's 'kisha club' system and how does it affect press freedom?
options: An accreditation system that limits press access to government briefings to established outlets
A licensing board for foreign correspondents
quiz.explanation: Japan's kisha club (press club) system restricts government briefing access to accredited established outlets, effectively excluding freelancers, foreign press, and digital-only outlets from key information sources — a structural barrier to journalistic diversity.

laws.title: Act on Specified Commercial Transactions and Platform Transparency
laws.subtitle: Japan has updated digital platform regulations including operator transparency requirements
laws.fullDescription: Japan's Act on Specified Commercial Transactions was updated to cover digital platforms. Japan passed the Act on Improving Transparency and Fairness in Trading on Specified Digital Platforms (2020) requiring large e-commerce and app store platforms to disclose their trading conditions and allow regulatory oversight. Japan's Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA) was significantly amended in 2022 to add rights similar to GDPR. The Act on Promotion of Ensuring Transparency for Social Media Platforms (2024) requires large platforms to explain their content moderation processes. Japan is developing an AI governance framework through METI.
laws.penalty: Transparency Act violations: fines and mandatory disclosure; updated PIPA: up to ¥100 million fines for organizations
exceptions: Research and journalism exemptions under PIPA

quiz.q: What does Japan's 2024 Act on Social Media Platform Transparency require platforms to do?
quiz.explanation: Japan's 2024 Act on Promoting Transparency for Social Media Platforms requires large platforms to explain their content moderation processes to users and the government — a transparency requirement designed to make algorithmic and editorial decisions more accountable without mandating specific outcomes.

laws.title: FSA Crypto Exchange Registration & Banking Act Reforms
laws.subtitle: Japan pioneered crypto exchange licensing after Mt. Gox collapse
laws.fullDescription: Japan's Financial Services Agency (FSA) was among the first regulators globally to create a formal crypto exchange registration system following the 2014 Mt. Gox collapse and 2018 Coincheck hack. All crypto exchanges must register with the FSA, maintain separate customer asset custody, implement robust cybersecurity, and conduct AML/KYC checks. Japan classifies crypto as 'crypto assets' (not currency) under the Payment Services Act. The Banking Act was amended to allow bank holding companies to invest in fintech. Japan's banking system features three megabanks (MUFG, SMFG, Mizuho) alongside Japan Post Bank and regional banks.
laws.penalty: Unregistered crypto exchange operation: up to 3 years imprisonment or ¥3 million fine; licensed exchange AML violations: business suspension orders and fines up to ¥10 million
exceptions: Crypto used within specific closed gaming ecosystems may have modified rules
Stablecoins issued by licensed institutions have separate regulatory path
Cross-border transactions with FSA-recognized foreign regulators may have simplified rules

quiz.q: What catastrophic event in 2014 prompted Japan to pioneer cryptocurrency exchange regulation?
quiz.explanation: The 2014 collapse of Mt. Gox, then the world's largest Bitcoin exchange handling 70% of global BTC transactions, prompted Japan's FSA to create the world's first formal crypto exchange registration and oversight system.

laws.title: Japan's Food Sanitation Act & Strict Additive Standards
laws.subtitle: Japan has the world's most restrictive food additive permitted list
laws.fullDescription: Japan's Food Sanitation Act (Shokuhin Eisei Hō) is enforced by the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) and Japan's Food Safety Commission. Japan maintains one of the world's most restrictive permitted food additive lists — many additives approved in the US and EU are not permitted in Japan. Japan also has strict pesticide residue limits (often stricter than Codex Alimentarius standards). Japan's food labeling law (implemented fully by 2023) requires detailed origin labeling for food items. Japan has a unique focus on food safety culture: traditional Japanese food safety is embedded in culinary training — sushi chefs undergo years of training partly around food safety. Japan's fugu (pufferfish) may only be prepared by licensed chefs due to tetrodotoxin poisoning risk.
laws.penalty: Food Sanitation Act violations: fines up to ¥3 million or 3 years imprisonment for manufacturers; selling food with non-permitted additives: product recall and business suspension; fugu preparation without license: criminal charges
exceptions: Traditional Japanese fermented foods (miso, soy sauce, sake) have specific designated additive rules
Natural food additives derived from traditional processes have modified approval pathways
Import food meeting WHO/Codex standards may require additional MHLW review before market entry

quiz.q: What unique food safety requirement governs the preparation of fugu (pufferfish) in Japan?
options: Fugu must be purchased frozen from certified distributors only
Only licensed chefs who have passed a specific certification exam may prepare fugu due to tetrodotoxin poisoning risk
Fugu must be served within 2 hours of preparation under refrigerated conditions
All fugu must be tested by government inspectors before service
quiz.explanation: Fugu (pufferfish) contains tetrodotoxin — a potent neurotoxin with no antidote — in its organs. Japanese law requires that only chefs who have passed a rigorous government certification exam (studying anatomy, preparation, and safety for 2-3 years under a licensed chef) may prepare and serve fugu to the public.

laws.title: Japan Animal Welfare Law — Pet Industry Regulation
laws.subtitle: Japan tightened pet industry regulations after 'eight-week rule'
laws.fullDescription: Japan's Act on Welfare and Management of Animals (動物の愛護及び管理に関する法律, 1973, amended 2019) prohibits animal cruelty and requires care standards. Japan's 2019 amendment was significant — it introduced an 'eight-week rule' prohibiting the sale of puppies and kittens under 8 weeks old, addressed online pet sales (all sellers must now show animals to buyers in person), and strengthened penalties. Japan has a massive pet industry but has struggled with 'puppy mill' problems. Japan bans animal fighting and has specific dolphin protections. The Taiji dolphin hunt remains controversial internationally. Japan also has strict import regulations protecting endemic wildlife. Enforcement is by local government veterinary officers.
laws.penalty: Animal cruelty: up to 5 years imprisonment or 5 million JPY fine (increased in 2019); abandonment: up to 1 year or 1 million JPY; business violations: fines
exceptions: Livestock farming under animal husbandry standards
Licensed whaling under contested IWC status
Scientific research with ethics approval
Traditional fishing practices
laws.sourceLabel: 動物の愛護及び管理に関する法律 (Act on Welfare and Management of Animals)

quiz.q: What major change did Japan's 2019 animal welfare amendment make regarding pet sales?
options: It introduced an eight-week rule prohibiting sale of puppies and kittens under 8 weeks old
It required pet stores to only sell Japanese breeds
It banned all online pet advertising
quiz.explanation: Japan's 2019 Animal Welfare Act amendment introduced the 'eight-week rule' prohibiting the sale of puppies and kittens under 8 weeks old, and required all pet sellers to show animals to buyers in person — addressing widespread criticism of Japan's puppy mill industry.

laws.title: Japan Civil Code — Surname Change Requirement and Same-Sex Marriage Debate
laws.subtitle: Japan requires married couples to share a surname — typically the husband's
laws.fullDescription: Japan's Civil Code (Minpō) requires married couples to share a surname — in practice, about 95% of couples adopt the husband's name. This requirement has been consistently criticized as discriminatory against women, who disproportionately change their names. The Supreme Court has upheld it twice (2015, 2021), saying it's for Parliament to change. Same-sex marriage is not legally recognized in Japan, though multiple lower courts have ruled the prohibition unconstitutional. Several Japanese cities and prefectures issue non-legally-binding 'partnership certificates.' Divorce: Japan allows kyōgi rikkon (divorce by agreement) through administrative registration — one of the world's simplest divorce processes. Divorce rates are significant. Japanese family courts (katei saibansho) handle custody disputes.
laws.penalty: Civil enforcement; koseki (family registry) system tracks all changes; child support ('yōiku-hi') enforcement is weak — a major policy concern; criminal domestic violence charges
exceptions: International couples can maintain different surnames under some conditions
Unofficial partnerships recognized in some municipalities
Adopted persons may retain birth surname
laws.sourceLabel: 日本民法 — 親族・相続 (Japanese Civil Code — Family Law)

quiz.q: What controversial marriage requirement does Japan's Civil Code maintain?
options: Married couples must share a surname — typically the husband's (upheld by Supreme Court twice)
Marriages must receive family consent from both sides
quiz.explanation: Japan's Civil Code requires married couples to share one surname — and in practice, about 95% of women change to the husband's name. The Supreme Court upheld this requirement in 2015 and 2021 despite criticism as discriminatory, saying Parliament should act. Multiple reform proposals have failed to pass in the Japanese Diet.

laws.title: Japan Shakuya Hoken Ho & Property Rights
laws.subtitle: Borrower's protection act and land ownership rules
laws.fullDescription: Japan's Shakuya Hoken Ho (Borrowers' Protection Act, 1991, revised 2000) provides comprehensive tenant protections, creating 'ordinary contracts' (automatically renewed unless landlord gives six-month notice with legitimate reason) and 'fixed-term contracts' (teikishakuya) with set end dates. Landlords seeking to terminate must show 'valid reason' (seito jiyuu), typically requiring significant relocation compensation (tachinokiryo). Japan's property market is unique in that buildings depreciate rapidly (typical 30-year lifespan in assessments), while land retains value. Foreign ownership of land is largely unrestricted.
laws.penalty: Eviction without just cause: illegal; landlord must pay relocation compensation; no general rent control
exceptions: Ordinary contracts protect tenants with automatic renewal rights
Fixed-term contracts (teikishakuya) have definite end dates with no renewal right

quiz.q: What unusual depreciation rule applies to buildings in Japan's property assessment system?
options: Buildings depreciate rapidly (30-year typical lifespan in assessments)
quiz.explanation: Japan's property valuation system depreciates building value rapidly, with a typical 30-year lifespan for wooden structures in official assessments, while land retains its value — making land the primary component of property value in Japan.

laws.title: Japan Consumer Contract Act & Consumer Affairs Agency
laws.subtitle: Consumer contract law and specialized consumer agency
laws.fullDescription: Japan established a dedicated Consumer Affairs Agency (CAA) in 2009 after several major food labeling and product safety scandals. The Consumer Contract Act (2000, amended 2022) provides rights to cancel contracts obtained through deception, undue pressure, or exploitation of psychological vulnerability. Japan has an 8-day cooling-off period for door-to-door sales and multi-level marketing contracts (Tokutei Shoho Torihiki Ho). The 2022 amendments addressed targeting of vulnerable consumers through social isolation techniques (prominent in cult-related cases). The National Consumer Affairs Center of Japan (NCAC) provides information and mediates complaints. Japan's PL Law (Product Liability Act, 1994) imposes strict liability for product defects.
laws.penalty: Consumer Contract Act violation: contract voidable; PL Law: strict product liability without proving negligence; door-to-door: 8-day cooling off
exceptions: 2022 amendment targets psychological manipulation of vulnerable consumers
Consumer Affairs Agency established 2009 after major scandals
laws.source: Consumer Contract Act 2000; Tokutei Shoho Torihiki Ho; PL Law 1994

quiz.q: What prompted Japan to establish its dedicated Consumer Affairs Agency (CAA) in 2009?
options: EU pressure for consumer law harmonization
Several major food labeling and product safety scandals
Trade friction with the United States
quiz.explanation: Japan established the Consumer Affairs Agency (CAA) in 2009 following a series of major food labeling fraud scandals (such as beef mislabeling) and product safety incidents that exposed gaps in the fragmented consumer protection system across multiple ministries.

laws.title: 日本国憲法 — Constitution of Japan (1947)
laws.subtitle: The postwar pacifist constitution drafted under US occupation
laws.fullDescription: Japan's 1947 Constitution, drafted under American occupation after WWII, has never been amended — making it the world's oldest unamended constitution. Article 9 famously renounces war and prohibits maintaining war potential, though the Self-Defense Forces (自衛隊) exist in legal tension with this clause. The Emperor is defined as 'the symbol of the State' with no political power. The constitution guarantees extensive civil rights. Debate over revising Article 9 has been ongoing under successive LDP governments, particularly under Shinzo Abe's administration.
laws.penalty: Constitutional violations adjudicated by Supreme Court. No explicit enforcement mechanism for Article 9 — political and legal debate ongoing.
exceptions: Self-Defense Forces justified as 'minimum necessary' defensive capability
Collective self-defense reinterpreted by cabinet resolution in 2015
US-Japan Security Treaty obligations coexist with Article 9 constraints
laws.sourceLabel: 最高裁判所 — Supreme Court of Japan

quiz.q: What makes Japan's 1947 Constitution uniquely remarkable among major world constitutions?
options: It was the first constitution to guarantee women's suffrage
It has never been amended since its adoption
It established the world's first parliamentary monarchy
quiz.explanation: Japan's constitution has remained unamended since 1947 — over 75 years — making it the world's longest-serving unamended constitution for a major nation. Article 9's war renunciation clause has been particularly controversial but has survived all amendment attempts.

laws.title: 自衛隊法 — Self-Defense Forces Act
laws.subtitle: Legal framework for Japan's military forces
laws.fullDescription: The Self-Defense Forces Act (1954) established Japan's Ground, Maritime, and Air Self-Defense Forces. Despite Article 9's war renunciation, Japan maintains one of the world's most capable defense forces with an annual budget exceeding ¥6 trillion. The SDF may only be deployed for 'defense of Japan' and international peacekeeping under strict conditions. PM Kishida's 2022 National Security Strategy dramatically shifted Japan's defense posture, doubling the defense budget to 2% of GDP by 2027 and acquiring counterstrike capabilities — a significant departure from postwar pacifism.
laws.penalty: Illegal deployment of SDF requires Diet authorization. Civilian control strictly maintained — military acting without civilian orders faces criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Disaster relief operations authorized without Diet approval
UN peacekeeping missions authorized under PKO Law
2015 security legislation allows limited collective self-defense
laws.sourceLabel: 防衛省 — Ministry of Defense Japan

quiz.q: What significant defense policy shift did Japan announce in 2022?
options: Complete abolition of the Self-Defense Forces
Doubling defense budget to 2% of GDP and acquiring counterstrike capabilities
Joining NATO as an observer member
Deploying troops abroad for the first time
quiz.explanation: Japan's 2022 National Security Strategy marked a historic shift: doubling defense spending to 2% of GDP and acquiring counterstrike ('enemy base strike') capabilities — fundamentally changing Japan's postwar pacifist defense posture.

laws.title: 会社法 — Companies Act of Japan
laws.subtitle: Corporate law governing Japanese business entities
laws.fullDescription: Japan's Companies Act (会社法, 2005) governs all forms of business corporations including kabushiki kaisha (KK, stock companies) and godo kaisha (LLC equivalent). A KK is the standard form for large businesses and requires at minimum one director. The Act was amended in 2019 and 2021 to strengthen corporate governance, requiring large listed companies to appoint audit and supervisory committees, and enabling electronic general meetings. Japan's corporate governance code (implemented by Tokyo Stock Exchange) pushes companies to appoint independent outside directors.
laws.penalty: Directors breaching fiduciary duties face civil liability for damages. Criminal penalties for fraudulent financial reporting up to 10 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Small companies (capital under ¥5M) have simplified requirements
Family businesses may operate as godo kaisha with less regulatory burden
Foreign companies may operate via branch office without establishing Japanese entity
laws.sourceLabel: 法務省 — Ministry of Justice Japan

quiz.q: What is the most common form of company for large businesses in Japan?
quiz.explanation: Kabushiki kaisha (KK) — the stock company — is the standard corporate form for large Japanese businesses. It provides limited liability and is analogous to a corporation or public limited company in other jurisdictions.

laws.title: 労働基準法 — Labor Standards Act
laws.subtitle: Core worker protections including overtime and leave
laws.fullDescription: Japan's Labor Standards Act (1947) establishes minimum working conditions: 8-hour workdays, 40-hour workweeks, paid annual leave (minimum 10 days after 6 months), and overtime limits. Japan's infamous overwork culture (過労死, karoshi — death from overwork) led to 2018 Work Style Reform legislation capping overtime at 100 hours/month and 720 hours/year. Labor inspections enforce these standards. Japan guarantees 10-20 days annual leave depending on tenure, though actual usage rates remain among the lowest in developed nations due to cultural pressure.
laws.penalty: Employers violating overtime caps face fines up to ¥300,000 per violation. Systematic violations result in criminal charges and public naming.
exceptions: Managers and supervisors partially exempt from overtime limits
Highly skilled professionals under discretionary work system
Certain IT and creative workers under planning work system
laws.sourceLabel: 厚生労働省 — Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare

quiz.q: What phenomenon prompted Japan's 2018 Work Style Reform legislation?
options: Mass unemployment during the Lost Decade
Karoshi — death from overwork — becoming a recognized national crisis
quiz.explanation: Karoshi (過労死) — death from overwork through cardiovascular disease or suicide — became a recognized public health crisis in Japan. High-profile deaths and lawsuits pushed the government to legislate the 2018 Work Style Reform, capping overtime at 100 hours/month.

laws.title: 刑法 — Penal Code of Japan
laws.subtitle: Japan's criminal law framework with emphasis on confession culture
laws.fullDescription: Japan's Penal Code (1907, extensively revised) defines crimes and punishments. The criminal justice system has a 99.9% conviction rate — prosecutors only bring cases they are virtually certain to win, and acquittals are extremely rare. The system has been criticized for excessive pretrial detention (最長23日, up to 23 days without charge), denial of attorney access during interrogation, and pressure to confess. Capital punishment (絞首刑, hanging) is retained and applied in secret — condemned prisoners are not given advance notice of their execution date.
laws.penalty: Murder: death penalty or life imprisonment. Robbery resulting in death: death or life. Drug trafficking: up to life imprisonment. White-collar fraud: up to 10 years.
exceptions: Juvenile offenders under 14 tried under Family Court Act
Mental incapacity recognized as defense
Statute of limitations applies to most crimes except murder
laws.sourceLabel: 法務省 — Ministry of Justice Japan

quiz.q: What is Japan's criminal conviction rate, and why is it so high?
options: 99.9% — prosecutors only charge cases they are virtually certain to win
quiz.explanation: Japan's 99.9% conviction rate reflects prosecutorial discretion: Japanese prosecutors only charge defendants when evidence is overwhelming. Critics argue this creates pressure to confess, since acquittals are so rare that defendants feel resistance is futile.

laws.title: 金融商品取引法 — Financial Instruments and Exchange Act
laws.subtitle: Securities regulation and insider trading prohibition
laws.fullDescription: Japan's FIEA (金商法, 2006) regulates securities markets, investment vehicles, and financial advisors. The Financial Services Agency (金融庁, FSA) supervises compliance. Insider trading (インサイダー取引) is criminally prohibited: trading on material non-public information carries up to 5 years imprisonment and ¥5 million fine. Japan's securities markets are supervised by the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC). High-frequency trading and cryptocurrency exchanges are regulated under 2020 amendments. Japan was among the first countries to establish a comprehensive crypto exchange licensing regime.
laws.penalty: Insider trading: up to 5 years imprisonment, ¥5M fine. Market manipulation: up to 10 years, ¥30M fine. Failure to file disclosure: up to 5 years.
exceptions: Certain institutional trades under portfolio rebalancing programs
Block trades with advance disclosure to FSA
Employees with options vesting on predetermined schedule
laws.sourceLabel: 金融庁 — Financial Services Agency Japan

quiz.q: What made Japan notable in cryptocurrency regulation?
options: Japan banned all cryptocurrency trading in 2017
Japan was among the first countries to license cryptocurrency exchanges
Japan created its own national cryptocurrency
Japan imposed a 100% capital gains tax on crypto
quiz.explanation: After the 2014 Mt. Gox collapse (then the world's largest Bitcoin exchange, based in Tokyo), Japan enacted comprehensive crypto exchange licensing requirements in 2017 — one of the world's first regulatory frameworks for cryptocurrency businesses.

laws.title: 借地借家法 — Land and Building Lease Act
laws.subtitle: Tenant and landlord rights in Japanese property law
laws.fullDescription: Japan's Land and Building Lease Act (1991) heavily protects tenants. Standard residential leases (普通借家契約) automatically renew and are nearly impossible for landlords to terminate without 'just cause' — which is interpreted very strictly. Fixed-term leases (定期借家契約) allow non-renewal but require notarized contracts. Japan's property market is unusual: buildings depreciate to near-zero value in 20-30 years (wooden structures) or 47 years (concrete), while land holds value. This depreciation schedule, combined with strong tenant protections, makes real estate investment dynamics very different from Western markets.
laws.penalty: Illegal eviction is a criminal offense. Landlords who harass tenants to vacate (嫌がらせ退去) face civil damages and potentially criminal charges.
exceptions: Fixed-term leases (定期借家) allow non-renewal if properly documented
Landlords can terminate for substantial non-payment (3+ months)
Government can compulsorily purchase land for public projects with compensation
laws.sourceLabel: 国土交通省 — Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism

quiz.q: What is unusual about how buildings are valued in Japan's property market?
options: Buildings appreciate faster than land in Japan
Buildings depreciate to near-zero value in 20-47 years while land holds value
All property in Japan is leased from the government
Foreign ownership of property is prohibited
quiz.explanation: Japanese buildings are valued on aggressive depreciation schedules — wooden buildings near-zero after 20-30 years, concrete after 47 years. Land holds value, but this means buying an existing house often means paying mainly for land, not structure — unique among major property markets.

laws.title: 環境基本法 — Basic Environment Act
laws.subtitle: Japan's foundational environmental protection framework
laws.fullDescription: Japan's Basic Environment Act (1993) replaced the 1967 pollution-era Basic Law for Environmental Pollution Control. Japan suffered catastrophic industrial pollution in the 1950s-70s: Minamata disease (mercury poisoning from Chisso chemical plant), Itai-itai disease (cadmium poisoning), and Yokkaichi asthma (sulfur dioxide from petrochemical complex). These tragedies drove Japan to develop world-leading environmental standards. The Act establishes polluter-pays principle and government environmental quality standards. Japan committed to carbon neutrality by 2050 and 46% emissions reduction by 2030 under the Paris Agreement.
laws.penalty: Industrial pollution violations under specific laws: up to 3 years imprisonment and ¥3M fines for companies, plus civil liability for health damages.
exceptions: Special economic zones may have modified environmental standards
Legacy pollution from pre-Act era addressed through separate compensation schemes
Agricultural burning of crop residues regulated by prefecture
laws.sourceLabel: 環境省 — Ministry of the Environment Japan

quiz.q: What notorious industrial disaster drove Japan to develop strict environmental law?
options: The 1954 Bikini Atoll nuclear fallout on Japanese fishermen
Minamata disease — mercury poisoning causing severe neurological damage
The 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake industrial fires
quiz.explanation: Minamata disease, caused by Chisso Corporation dumping mercury into Minamata Bay from 1932-1968, caused severe neurological damage, birth defects, and death in thousands. Combined with other industrial pollution disasters, it galvanized Japan's environmental movement and led to world-leading pollution controls.

laws.title: 出入国管理及び難民認定法 — Immigration Control Act
laws.subtitle: Japan's strict immigration and refugee recognition system
laws.fullDescription: Japan's Immigration Control and Refugee Recognition Act tightly controls entry and residence. Japan maintains among the world's lowest refugee recognition rates — under 1% of applications accepted compared to 30-60% in European countries. Japan accepted only 202 refugees in 2022 despite receiving 3,772 applications. The system has been criticized for indefinite detention of asylum seekers. A 2023 immigration law revision allows deportation of those who apply for asylum multiple times, which critics say deters legitimate refugees. Work visas are category-specific and switching visa types is difficult.
laws.penalty: Overstaying visa: deportation and 5-year re-entry ban. Illegal employment of foreigners: employer fined up to ¥3M and 3 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Highly Skilled Professional visa (HSP) provides fast-track permanent residency
Japanese citizens' foreign spouses receive spousal visa with relatively easy renewal
UNHCR-referred refugees receive expedited consideration
laws.sourceLabel: 出入国在留管理庁 — Immigration Services Agency

quiz.q: How does Japan's refugee recognition rate compare internationally?
options: Japan accepts refugees at the OECD average rate of ~35%
Japan accepts under 1% of applications vs 30-60% in European countries
Japan has the highest per-capita refugee acceptance in Asia
Japan has no formal refugee recognition system
quiz.explanation: Japan's refugee recognition rate is extraordinarily low — often under 1% — compared to 30-60% acceptance rates in European nations. Japan accepted only 202 refugees in 2022 despite receiving 3,772 applications, making it one of the most restrictive developed nations for asylum seekers.

laws.title: 個人情報の保護に関する法律 — Act on Protection of Personal Information
laws.subtitle: Japan's comprehensive data privacy framework
laws.fullDescription: Japan's APPI (個人情報保護法, 2003, major revisions 2017, 2022) regulates collection and use of personal data. The Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC) enforces compliance. The 2022 revision strengthened requirements: mandatory breach notification within 3-5 days, right to request deletion of personal data, and extraterritorial application to foreign companies handling Japanese personal data. Japan achieved EU adequacy status in 2019 — enabling free flow of personal data between Japan and the EU. Anonymized and pseudonymized data have separate regulatory tracks.
laws.penalty: Intentional violations: up to 1 year imprisonment, ¥1M fine for individuals. Corporate violations: up to ¥100M fine under 2022 amendments.
exceptions: Academic research, journalism, and religious organizations have modified requirements
Personal data processing for statistical purposes with proper anonymization
Government agencies covered by separate Public Sector law
laws.sourceLabel: 個人情報保護委員会 — Personal Information Protection Commission

quiz.q: What significant international recognition did Japan's data protection law receive in 2019?
options: Japan joined the Five Eyes intelligence sharing agreement
Japan achieved EU adequacy status enabling free data flow with EU
Japan's law became the template for Asia-Pacific data standards
Japan signed the APEC Cross-Border Privacy Rules system
quiz.explanation: In 2019, Japan achieved EU adequacy status — meaning the EU recognized Japan's data protection as providing equivalent protection to GDPR standards. This enables free flow of personal data between Japan and EU member states without additional safeguards.

laws.title: 道路交通法 — Road Traffic Act
laws.subtitle: Traffic laws and Japan's zero-tolerance drunk driving rules
laws.fullDescription: Japan has extremely strict drunk driving laws under the Road Traffic Act. The legal blood alcohol limit is 0.03% for drivers — half of the 0.08% limit common in many countries — and even lower for commercial drivers. There is a separate offense for driving 'under the influence' (影響で運転) vs 'drunk driving' (酒気帯び運転). Critically, passengers who knowingly allow or encourage a drunk person to drive also face criminal liability, as do establishments that serve alcohol to a known driver. This 'drunk driving chain' liability effectively outsources enforcement to social pressure.
laws.penalty: Drunk driving: up to 5 years imprisonment or ¥1M fine. Causing death/injury while drunk: up to 20 years. Passengers who permitted drunk driving: up to 3 years.
exceptions: Medical necessity allowing blood alcohol above limit (rare)
Emergency situations may mitigate penalty at judge's discretion
First-time minor offenses may result in license suspension rather than prosecution
laws.sourceLabel: 警察庁 — National Police Agency Japan

quiz.q: What unique aspect of Japan's drunk driving law extends liability beyond just the driver?
options: Car manufacturers are liable if safety systems fail to prevent drunk driving
Passengers who knowingly allow a drunk driver to drive face criminal charges
Bars are automatically liable for any accidents by patrons
Road designers are liable if curves contribute to drunk driving accidents
quiz.explanation: Japan's 'drunk driving chain' liability holds passengers criminally liable if they knowingly permitted or encouraged a drunk person to drive. Establishments serving known drivers also face liability. This social-pressure enforcement mechanism has been credited with dramatically reducing drunk driving fatalities.

laws.title: 民法 — Civil Code: Family Law Provisions
laws.subtitle: Marriage, divorce, and family law in Japan
laws.fullDescription: Japan's Civil Code family law provisions include uniquely controversial elements. Japan requires married couples to share a surname — in practice overwhelmingly meaning women adopt their husband's name (95% of cases). This has been challenged constitutionally multiple times but the Supreme Court has upheld it, citing 'social order'. The government has debated allowing separate surnames for decades without resolution. Japan also prohibits remarriage for women within 100 days of divorce (to establish paternity), recently reduced from 180 days and being reconsidered. Same-sex marriage is not recognized at the national level, though several cities grant partnership certificates.
laws.penalty: Bigamy: up to 2 years imprisonment. Marriage registration violations: administrative fines. Non-compliance with surname requirements prevents official registration.
exceptions: Foreigners marrying Japanese nationals may retain foreign name in home country records
Common-law marriage (内縁) has some but not all legal protections
Corporate name retention allowed in professional contexts
laws.sourceLabel: 法務省 — Ministry of Justice Japan

quiz.q: What controversial requirement does Japan's Civil Code impose on married couples?
options: All marriages must be registered at a Shinto shrine
Couples must share a surname — effectively requiring most women to change their name
Couples must reside together continuously for 1 year before legal marriage
Marriage requires parental consent until age 25
quiz.explanation: Japan's Civil Code requires married couples to share a single surname. Since 95% of couples choose the husband's name, this effectively requires most women to abandon their birth name. Despite decades of debate and multiple court challenges, this requirement remains — making Japan the only G7 country without separate surname options.

laws.title: 健康保険法 — National Health Insurance Act
laws.subtitle: Japan's universal health coverage system
laws.fullDescription: Japan has achieved near-universal health coverage (国民皆保険) since 1961. All residents must enroll in either employer-based health insurance (社会保険) or National Health Insurance (国民健康保険). Patients pay 30% of medical costs (10% for elderly over 75) up to a monthly maximum cap (高額療養費制度) — beyond which insurance covers everything. Japan has the highest number of MRI machines per capita in the world and doctor visits are among the most frequent. The system faces pressure from an aging population: by 2025, the baby-boom '団塊世代' generation all reached 75+.
laws.penalty: Failing to enroll in health insurance: retrospective premiums charged. Employers failing to enroll employees: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Life-on-public-assistance (生活保護) recipients covered separately by social welfare
Overseas Japanese temporarily exempt while abroad
Foreign visitors not required to enroll for short stays
laws.sourceLabel: 厚生労働省 — Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare

quiz.q: What innovative cost-protection feature exists in Japan's health insurance system?
options: All medical care is completely free for all residents
Monthly out-of-pocket costs are capped — insurance covers everything beyond that maximum
Patients never pay anything at the point of care
Only preventive care is covered; treatment must be privately purchased
quiz.explanation: Japan's 高額療養費制度 (high-cost medical expense system) caps monthly out-of-pocket costs based on income level. Once a patient's monthly medical costs exceed the cap (approximately ¥80,000-100,000 for average earners), insurance covers all remaining costs — protecting against catastrophic medical expenses.

laws.title: 教育基本法 — Fundamental Law of Education
laws.subtitle: Japan's constitutional framework for compulsory education
laws.fullDescription: Japan's Fundamental Law of Education (2006, revising the 1947 occupation-era law) governs the education system. Education is compulsory for ages 6-15 (elementary + middle school, 9 years). Japan's school system is internationally renowned for academic achievement (PISA rankings consistently among top nations), universal literacy, and intense examination culture. The 受験戦争 (examination war) — particularly for university entrance — is a defining social phenomenon. The National Center for University Entrance Examinations (大学入学共通テスト) replaced the older セ試験 in 2021. Japan has high enrollment in private tutoring schools (塾, juku).
laws.penalty: Parents failing to enroll children in compulsory education: administrative warnings and fines. Private schools operating without authorization: closure orders.
exceptions: Home schooling in a gray area — technically permitted but attendance certificates required for certain purposes
Special education schools for students with disabilities
Foreign school students may follow their national curriculum
laws.sourceLabel: 文部科学省 — Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology

quiz.q: What is the '受験戦争' (juken sensou) in Japanese society?
options: A mandatory military examination for all 18-year-olds
The intensely competitive university entrance examination culture
An annual athletic competition between schools
quiz.explanation: 受験戦争 (examination war) describes Japan's intensely competitive university entrance examination culture. Students spend years preparing, often attending juku (cram schools) after regular school hours. Admission to top universities like Tokyo University virtually guarantees access to elite careers — making the stakes extremely high.

laws.title: 独占禁止法 — Antimonopoly Act
laws.subtitle: Japan's competition law and cartel prohibition
laws.fullDescription: Japan's Antimonopoly Act (私的独占の禁止及び公正取引の確保に関する法律, 1947) prohibits monopolization, unreasonable restraints of trade (cartels), and unfair trade practices. The Japan Fair Trade Commission (公正取引委員会, JFTC) enforces competition law. Japan has a unique system of keiretsu (系列) — cross-shareholding networks of companies — which have been debated as potentially anti-competitive. Famous cartels prosecuted include the 2000s construction cartel (談合, dango) involving massive bid-rigging on public works. Japan has a leniency program allowing cartel participants who self-report to reduce penalties.
laws.penalty: Criminal penalties for hardcore cartels: up to 5 years imprisonment and ¥5M fine for individuals; corporate surcharge up to 10% of affected sales for 3 years.
exceptions: Certain agricultural cooperatives exempt from specific provisions
Export cartels authorized under Export and Foreign Trade Act
Small business cooperatives have modified competition rules
laws.sourceLabel: 公正取引委員会 — Japan Fair Trade Commission

quiz.q: What unique Japanese business structure has been debated as potentially anti-competitive?
options: Keiretsu — networks of cross-shareholding companies with preferential business relationships
quiz.explanation: Keiretsu (系列) are networks of companies with interlocking shareholding and preferential business relationships — like banks, manufacturers, and suppliers all owning small stakes in each other and favoring each other for business. While Japan's JFTC monitors keiretsu for anti-competitive behavior, the structure itself remains legal.

laws.title: 原子力規制法 — Nuclear Regulation Act
laws.subtitle: Post-Fukushima nuclear safety regime in Japan
laws.fullDescription: The 2011 Fukushima Daiichi disaster — caused by the Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami — was the worst nuclear accident since Chernobyl, displacing 154,000 people and triggering a complete shutdown of Japan's nuclear fleet. The Nuclear Regulation Authority (原子力規制委員会, NRA) was created in 2012 to replace the discredited nuclear safety agencies. Under new regulations, nuclear plants must install filtered containment venting, tsunami barriers, and emergency command centers. Reactor restart requires NRA approval plus local government consent. As of 2023, about 12 of Japan's 33 operable reactors have restarted, with more pending, as Japan grapples with energy security.
laws.penalty: Operating nuclear facilities without authorization: severe criminal penalties. Safety violations: immediate shutdown orders and criminal investigation.
exceptions: Research reactors at universities face less stringent commercial rules
Decommissioning activities under separate regulatory track
Emergency procedures allow temporary rule modifications during declared nuclear emergency
laws.sourceLabel: 原子力規制委員会 — Nuclear Regulation Authority

quiz.q: What institutional change did the Fukushima disaster trigger in Japan's nuclear governance?
options: Japan abolished all nuclear power and committed to renewables only
The NRA was created to replace discredited agencies, requiring new safety standards for restarts
Japan nationalized all nuclear power plants
Japan signed a treaty permanently banning nuclear power
quiz.explanation: The Fukushima disaster exposed systemic failures in Japan's nuclear safety oversight, including regulators too close to industry (the 'nuclear village'). The Nuclear Regulation Authority was created in 2012 with greater independence. All reactors were shut down; restarts require NRA approval of new safety measures plus local government consent — a much higher bar than pre-Fukushima.

laws.title: 公職選挙法 — Public Offices Election Act
laws.subtitle: Campaign finance and election rules in Japan
laws.fullDescription: Japan's Public Offices Election Act (1950) regulates Diet (国会) and local elections. Japan has strict and unusual campaign restrictions: door-to-door canvassing is prohibited, campaign period strictly limited (12 days for House of Representatives), and campaign spending caps are tightly enforced. Social media campaigning was only permitted from 2013. Japan uses a mixed electoral system: single-member districts plus proportional representation for the Diet. Voter turnout has declined: Lower House elections often see 50-55% turnout. Political funding is regulated under the Political Funds Control Act, though scandals involving 'slush funds' (裏金) repeatedly emerge.
laws.penalty: Election law violations: up to 3 years imprisonment. Vote-buying: up to 3 years. Campaign spending violations: fines and potential seat invalidation.
exceptions: Political parties receive public funding based on vote share
Incumbents may maintain 'district offices' year-round distinct from campaign offices
Certain agricultural cooperatives' political activities treated separately
laws.sourceLabel: 総務省 — Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications

quiz.q: What unusual restriction does Japan's Public Offices Election Act impose on campaigns?
options: Candidates must be proposed by their employers
Door-to-door canvassing is prohibited during election campaigns
All campaign materials must be in Japanese only
Candidates must pass a written test on policy
quiz.explanation: Japan's election law prohibits door-to-door canvassing (訪問運動) — a fundamental campaign tactic in most democracies. Combined with strictly limited campaign periods (just 12 days for Lower House elections), Japan's election law restricts direct voter contact in ways unusual among developed democracies.

laws.title: 銃砲刀剣類所持等取締法 — Firearms and Swords Control Act
laws.subtitle: Japan's near-total prohibition on civilian firearms
laws.fullDescription: Japan's Firearms and Swords Control Act virtually prohibits civilian possession of firearms. Licensed hunters may possess shotguns after extensive background checks, mental health assessments, written exams, storage requirements, and police inspection. Handguns are essentially banned for civilians entirely. Japan consistently has among the world's lowest gun death rates: 10 deaths per year in a nation of 125 million (compared to 45,000+ annually in the US). The July 2022 assassination of former PM Shinzo Abe by a homemade shotgun shocked Japan precisely because gun violence is so alien to Japanese society.
laws.penalty: Illegal possession of a firearm: up to 15 years imprisonment (up to 10 for ammunition alone). Manufacturing firearms: up to 15 years.
exceptions: Licensed hunters may possess shotguns and air rifles under strict conditions
Olympic and competition shooters authorized for sport shooting
Police and Self-Defense Forces armed through separate government provisions
laws.sourceLabel: 警察庁 — National Police Agency Japan

quiz.q: What event in 2022 particularly shocked Japan because of its extreme rarity?
options: A terrorist bombing in Tokyo's subway
The assassination of former PM Shinzo Abe by a homemade shotgun
A mass stabbing at a Tokyo elementary school
A police officer being killed in the line of duty
quiz.explanation: The July 2022 assassination of former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe by a man using a homemade shotgun shocked Japan profoundly — not because political violence is entirely unknown, but because gun violence is so extraordinarily rare in Japan (fewer than 10 firearm deaths per year) that the use of any firearm in a crime is national news.

laws.title: 消費税法 — Consumption Tax Act
laws.subtitle: Japan's VAT system and its economic implications
laws.fullDescription: Japan's consumption tax (消費税) was introduced in 1989 at 3%, raised to 5% in 1997, 8% in 2014, and 10% in 2019. The tax is a central political battlefield: the 1997 increase contributed to a recession, and PM Abe delayed the 2019 increase twice due to economic concerns. A reduced 8% rate applies to food and beverages (except restaurant consumption) and newspaper subscriptions. Japan's consumption tax is low by international standards — the EU average VAT is ~21%. With a national debt exceeding 250% of GDP, successive governments have raised the consumption tax to fund social security as Japan's population ages.
laws.penalty: Tax evasion: up to 10 years imprisonment and ¥10M fine. Failure to file: administrative penalties and mandatory interest charges.
exceptions: Export sales zero-rated (consumption tax refunded for exports)
Medical services, school tuition, and welfare services exempt
Small businesses under ¥10M annual sales exempt from collecting consumption tax
laws.sourceLabel: 国税庁 — National Tax Agency Japan

quiz.q: Why is Japan's 10% consumption tax considered low by international standards?
options: Japan has the most regressive tax system in the G7
The EU average VAT is ~21%, making Japan's 10% modest despite political controversy
Japan compensates by having extremely high income tax
Japan's consumption tax only applies to luxury goods
quiz.explanation: Despite causing major political controversy each time it's raised, Japan's 10% consumption tax remains low by OECD standards — EU countries average ~21% VAT, with some as high as 27% (Hungary). Japan's aging population and massive public debt create pressure for further increases, but political resistance remains strong.

laws.title: 外国為替及び外国貿易法 — Foreign Exchange and Foreign Trade Act
laws.subtitle: Japan's controls on foreign investment in sensitive sectors
laws.fullDescription: Japan's FEFTA (外為法) regulates foreign exchange transactions and foreign direct investment in Japan. The Act was significantly strengthened in 2020 in response to concerns about foreign acquisition of sensitive technology companies. Foreign investors acquiring 1%+ stakes in 'core' industries (defense, nuclear, semiconductors, cybersecurity, broadcasting) must file pre-acquisition notifications with the Ministry of Finance and sector ministries. The threshold was lowered from 10% to 1%, dramatically expanding review scope. Japan applies heightened scrutiny to investments from countries of 'concern'.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized investments in sensitive sectors: compulsory divestiture orders, criminal penalties up to 3 years imprisonment and ¥1M fine.
exceptions: Portfolio investments under 1% threshold exempt from prior notification
Investments from countries with reciprocal agreements benefit from lighter review
Reinvestment of dividends by existing shareholders generally exempt
laws.sourceLabel: 財務省 — Ministry of Finance Japan

quiz.q: What foreign investment threshold triggers mandatory pre-notification in Japan's sensitive sectors?
options: 1% stake or more — lowered in 2020 amid security concerns
quiz.explanation: Japan lowered the foreign investment pre-notification threshold in sensitive industries from 10% to just 1% in 2020 — a sweeping expansion of national security review. This means acquiring even a very small stake in companies in defense, semiconductors, cybersecurity, or other 'core' sectors requires government approval in advance.
